claim: Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is the most common congenital cardiovascular disease in general population and is found in nearly 1.4% of the general population.
source: Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) disease is the most common congenital cardiovascular abnormality and is found in nearly 1.4% of the general population (Garg et al., 2005; Michelena et al., 2011; Verma and Siu, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Garg et al., 2005; Michelena et al., 2011; Verma and Siu, 2014).

claim: BAV is associated with an approximately 40% risk of developing thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA).
source: BAV arises from incomplete separation or fusion of the aortic valve cusps and is associated with an approximately 40% risk of developing thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA), namely, bicuspid aortopathy (Verma and Siu, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Verma and Siu, 2014.

claim: Progressive aneurysmal dilation can potentially develop into lethal dissection or rupture.
source: BAV-TAA poses a severe health threat to a large population because progressive aneurysmal dilation can potentially develop into lethal dissection or rupture (Goldfinger et al., 2014; Olsson et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Goldfinger et al., 2014; Olsson et al., 2006).

claim: The current clinical management of BAV-TAA mainly relies on prophylactic surgical repair of the notably dilated aorta.
source: The current clinical management mainly relies on prophylactic surgical repair of the notably dilated aorta (Coady et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Coady et al., 2010.

claim: There is an absence of effective pharmaceutical therapy to alleviate aortopathy progression due to incomplete understanding of pathophysiological mechanisms of BAV-TAA.
source: At present, the understanding of pathophysiological mechanisms of BAV-TAA is incomplete, which leads to the absence of effective pharmaceutical therapy to alleviate aortopathy progression (Lindeman and Matsumura, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lindeman and Matsumura, 2019.

claim: Genetic factors are considered to play a pivotal role in the disease progression of BAV-TAA.
source: In particular, genetic factors are considered to play a pivotal role in the disease progression (Isselbacher et al., 2016; Prakash et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Isselbacher et al., 2016; Prakash et al., 2014).

claim: NOTCH1 insufficiency has been observed in the population with BAV.
source: NOTCH1 insufficiency has been observed in the population with BAV (Balistreri et al., 2018; Harrison et al., 2019; Malashicheva et al., 2020; Sciacca et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published studies (Balistreri et al., 2018; Harrison et al., 2019; Malashicheva et al., 2020; Sciacca et al., 2013).

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been closely linked to a variety of cardiovascular disorders, such as heart failure and atherosclerosis.
source: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been closely linked to a variety of cardiovascular disorders, such as heart failure and atherosclerosis.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge without specific citations in this sentence.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction was related to the development of arterial aneurysm formation.
source: Recent studies found that mitochondrial dysfunction was also related to the development of arterial aneurysm formation (Cooper et al., 2021; van der Pluijm et al., 2018; Oller et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three recent studies (Cooper et al., 2021; van der Pluijm et al., 2018; Oller et al., 2021).

claim: A single-cell transcriptome analysis on aneurysmal human aortic tissue suggested that mitochondrial dysfunction and increased chromatin oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) were found in TAA tissues.
source: A single-cell transcriptome analysis on aneurysmal human aortic tissue suggested that mitochondrial dysfunction and increased chromatin oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) were found in TAA tissues and insufficient ATP production might not be sufficient for the contractile activities of human aortic smooth muscle cells (HAoSMCs) (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2020.

claim: Insufficient ATP production might not be sufficient for the contractile activities of human aortic smooth muscle cells (HAoSMCs) in TAA.
source: A single-cell transcriptome analysis on aneurysmal human aortic tissue suggested that mitochondrial dysfunction and increased chromatin oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) were found in TAA tissues and insufficient ATP production might not be sufficient for the contractile activities of human aortic smooth muscle cells (HAoSMCs) (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2020 and involves speculative reasoning about ATP sufficiency.

claim: A shift toward fission event is one of the main causes of mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Particularly, mitochondrial fission and fusion are dynamically balanced to maintain mitochondrial homeostasis and functions; and a shift toward fission event is one of the main causes of mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Impaired mitochondrial dynamics was found to play salient roles in abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) development in a mice model.
source: In a mice model of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), impaired mitochondrial dynamics was found to play salient roles in disease development, and could be attenuated by the mitochondrial fission inhibitor Mdivi1 (Cooper et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cooper et al., 2021.

claim: Impaired mitochondrial dynamics in AAA could be attenuated by the mitochondrial fission inhibitor Mdivi1.
source: In a mice model of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), impaired mitochondrial dynamics was found to play salient roles in disease development, and could be attenuated by the mitochondrial fission inhibitor Mdivi1 (Cooper et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cooper et al., 2021.

claim: There was close interaction between NOTCH1 signaling and homeostatic mitochondrial dynamics in the differentiation of cardiomyocytes.
source: It has been reported that there was close interaction between NOTCH1 signaling and homeostatic mitochondrial dynamics in the differentiation of cardiomyocytes (Kasahara et al., 2013) and the survival of breast cancer cells (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kasahara et al., 2013.

claim: There was close interaction between NOTCH1 signaling and homeostatic mitochondrial dynamics in the survival of breast cancer cells.
source: It has been reported that there was close interaction between NOTCH1 signaling and homeostatic mitochondrial dynamics in the differentiation of cardiomyocytes (Kasahara et al., 2013) and the survival of breast cancer cells (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2018.

claim: NOTCH1-haploinsufficient mice in a preliminary 129S6 background exhibited aortic root dilation but did not show BAV characteristics.
source: Although Koenig et al. generated NOTCH1-haploinsufficient mice in a preliminary 129S6 background that exhibited aortic root dilation, these mice did not show BAV characteristics (Koenig et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Koenig et al., 2017.

claim: Microfluidic-based organ-on-chip models have been widely developed to replicate human tissue microenvironment for toxicity analysis, drug screening and disease modeling.
source: Owing to the bioengineering advance, microfluidic-based organ-on-chip models have been widely developed to replicates human tissue microenvironment for toxicity analysis, drug screening and disease modeling and thus promotes pharmaceutical translation from preclinical studies to clinical trials (Zhang et al., 2018; Ingber, 2016; Park et al., 2019; Thacker et al., 2020; Hofemeier et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to five published studies (Zhang et al., 2018; Ingber, 2016; Park et al., 2019; Thacker et al., 2020; Hofemeier et al., 2021).

claim: H&E staining showed interrupted elastic fibers and thinning of the tunica media in the BAV-TAA aortas compared with non-diseased aortic tissue.
source: Hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) staining showed interrupted elastic fibers and thinning of the tunica media in the BAV-TAA aortas compared with non-diseased aortic tissue (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: NOTCH1 expression was significantly lower in BAV-TAA aortic tissues than in non-diseased aortic tissues.
source: A Western blotting analysis showed that NOTCH1 expression was significantly lower in BAV-TAA aortic tissues than in non-diseased aortic tissues.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting experimental data.

claim: SM22 and CNN1 expression was significantly reduced in BAV-TAA aortic tissues.
source: SM22 and CNN1 expression was significantly reduced in BAV-TAA aortic tissues (Figure 1b–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b-c.

claim: The protein expression of MFN1 and MFN2 was significantly lower in the BAV-TAA group than in the non-diseased group.
source: However, the protein expression of MFN1 and MFN2 was significantly lower in the BAV-TAA group than in the non-diseased group (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: MFN1 and MFN2 were expressed at low levels in tissues with NOTCH1 insufficiency.
source: In general, we found that MFN1 and MFN2 were expressed at low levels in tissues with NOTCH1 insufficiency (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The expression of NOTCH1 exhibited a positive correlation with MFN1 and MFN2 in aortic tissues.
source: The expression of NOTCH1 exhibited a positive correlation with MFN1 and MFN2 in aortic tissues.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: The expressions of DRP1 and MFF did not show a correlation with the expression of NOTCH1.
source: The expressions of DRP1 and MFF did not show a correlation with the expression of NOTCH1 (Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1e.

claim: In total, 70 upregulated proteins and 257 downregulated proteins were identified in BAV-TAA aortic tissues compared to non-diseased tissues.
source: In total, 70 upregulated proteins and 257 downregulated proteins were identified (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic analysis data.

claim: Acute phase response signaling, mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative phosphorylation pathways were significantly enriched in BAV-TAA aortic tissues.
source: The enriched canonical pathways identified by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) showed that acute phase response signaling, mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative phosphorylation pathways were significantly enriched in BAV-TAA aortic tissues (Figure 1f, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 1f and Supplementary file 1c.

claim: Z-score of oxidative phosphorylation pathway was −2.333, indicating significantly inhibited.
source: Among these pathways, Z-score of oxidative phosphorylation pathway was −2.333, indicating significantly inhibited.
evidence: The claim is supported by IPA analysis data.

claim: The aorta smooth muscle-on-a-chip model was composed of three chambers: a top vacuum chamber, a middle chamber containing culture medium, and a bottom vacuum chamber.
source: The model was composed of three chambers: (i) a top vacuum chamber deforming the upper PDMS membrane; (ii) a middle chamber containing the culture medium to maintain cell growth on the PDMS membranes; and (iii) a bottom vacuum chamber deforming the lower PDMS membrane.
evidence: The claim describes the design of the experimental model.

claim: The measured Young's elastic modulus values of the commercialized PDMS membrane were 1.71 MPa within 25% tensile strain and 1.67 MPa within 500% tensile strain.
source: The measured Young's elastic modulus values of the commercialized PDMS membrane were 1.71 MPa within 25% tensile strain and 1.67 MPa within 500% tensile strain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A vacuum pressure of 10 kPa induced 7.18 ± 0.44% strain.
source: A vacuum pressure of 10 kPa induced 7.18 ± 0.44% strain (7.09 ± 0.18% strain in the lower layer and 7.27 ± 0.28% strain in the upper layer)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: A vacuum pressure of 15 kPa induced 17.28 ± 0.91% strain.
source: and 15 kPa induced 17.28 ± 0.91% strain (17.29 ± 0.62% strain in the lower layer and 17.23 ± 0.64% strain in the upper layer) (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Rhythmic tensile strain induced a decrease in the cell width and an increase in the cell length in HAoSMCs.
source: Cytoskeletal F-actin staining images of HAoSMCs showed a decrease in the cell width and an increase in the cell length in the presence of rhythmic low or high strain (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by F-actin staining data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The length-to-width ratio increased from 2.33 ± 0.82 under static conditions to 2.74 ± 1.01 under low strain or 3.50 ± 1.19 under high strain.
source: The results also revealed an increase in the length-to-width ratio from 2.33 ± 0.82 under static conditions to 2.74 ± 1.01 under low strain or 3.50 ± 1.19 under high strain (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Cells tended to align perpendicularly to the direction of the applied strain with the angle between the directions of the cellular alignment and the applied strain being approximately 90°.
source: Compared with the irregular orientation of the cells observed under static culture, the cells tended to align perpendicularly to the direction of the applied strain. The angle between the directions of the cellular alignment and the applied strain was approximately 90° (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell alignment data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The contractile phenotype markers SM22 and CNN1 were upregulated under either low or high strain.
source: The results showed that the contractile phenotype markers SM22 and CNN1 were upregulated under either low or high strain (Figure 3e–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3e-f.

claim: The expression of the synthetic phenotypic marker OPN under both rhythmic low and high strain was lower than that observed under static conditions.
source: The expression of the synthetic phenotypic marker OPN under both rhythmic low and high strain was lower than that observed under static conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting experimental data.

claim: An approximately 60% reduction in NOTCH1 mRNA expression was found in the NOTCH1-KD group compared with the WT and NC groups.
source: An approximately 60% reduction in NOTCH1 mRNA expression was found in the NOTCH1-KD group compared with the WT and NC groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Under static conditions, the mRNA expression of SM22 and CNN1 was upregulated and that of OPN was downregulated in the NOTCH1-KD group compared with the WT and NC groups.
source: Under static conditions, the mRNA expression of SM22 and CNN1 was upregulated and that of OPN was downregulated in the NOTCH1-KD group compared with the WT and NC groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: SM22 and CNN1 were upregulated in the NOTCH-KD group compared with the WT group under static conditions.
source: As shown in Figure 4b–c, immunofluorescent staining images showed that SM22 and CNN1 were upregulated in the NOTCH-KD group compared with the WT group under static conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4b-c.

claim: The expression of SM22 and CNN1 in NOTCH-KD HAoSMCs was lower than that in the WT group under rhythmic strain conditions.
source: However, the opposite results were observed under rhythmic strain conditions: the expression of SM22 and CNN1 in NOTCH-KD HAoSMCs was lower than that in the WT group under rhythmic strain conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence experimental data.

claim: In WT HAoSMCs, rhythmic strain induced the upregulation of SM22 and CNN1 expression compared with the levels observed under static conditions.
source: In WT HAoSMCs, rhythmic strain induced the upregulation of SM22 and CNN1 expression compared with the levels observed under static conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting experimental data.

claim: A downregulation of SM22 and CNN1 expression was detected in NOTCH-KD HAoSMCs exposed to rhythmic strain.
source: However, a downregulation of SM22 and CNN1 expression was detected in NOTCH-KD HAoSMCs exposed to rhythmic strain.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting experimental data.

claim: The expression of MFN1 and MFN2 was downregulated in NOTCH1-KD HAoSMCs under static conditions.
source: As shown in Figure 5a–b, the expression of MFN1 and MFN2 was downregulated in NOTCH1-KD HAoSMCs under static conditions, and the expression of MFN2 presented a significant difference between the two groups.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 5a-b.

claim: DRP1 and MFF expression was significantly increased in NOTCH1-KD HAoSMCs under static conditions.
source: DRP1 and MFF expression was significantly increased in NOTCH1-KD HAoSMCs under static conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting experimental data.

claim: Rhythmic strain induced a decrease in MFN1 expression in the NOTCH1-KD group but an increase in the WT group.
source: Rhythmic strain induced a decrease in MFN1 expression in the NOTCH1-KD group but an increase in the WT group.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting experimental data.

claim: MFN2 expression was decreased in both the WT and NOTCH1-KD groups after exposure to rhythmic strain but was lower in the NOTCH1-KD group than in the WT group, particularly under rhythmic high strain conditions.
source: MFN2 expression was decreased in both the WT and NOTCH1-KD groups after exposure to rhythmic strain but was lower in the NOTCH1-KD group than in the WT group, particularly under rhythmic high strain conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting experimental data.

claim: Rhythmic strain induced an increase in DRP1 and MFF expression in both the WT and NOTCH1-KD groups.
source: Rhythmic strain induced an increase in DRP1 and MFF expression in both the WT and NOTCH1-KD groups, and DRP1 and MFF were highly expressed in NOTCH1-KD HAoSMCs under both rhythmic strain and static conditions (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Low or high strain induced a decrease in long rod-shaped elongated interconnected mitochondrial networks and a significant increase in spheroid-shaped fragmented mitochondrial morphology in both WT and NOTHC1-KD HAoSMCs, and these alterations were more frequent in NOTHC1-KD HAoSMCs under high strain conditions.
source: Low or high strain induced alterations of the mitochondrial shape in both WT and NOTHC1-KD HAoSMCs, and these alterations included both a decrease in long rod-shaped elongated interconnected mitochondrial networks and a significant increase in spheroid-shaped fragmented mitochondrial morphology and were more frequent in NOTHC1-KD HAoSMCs under high strain conditions (Figure 5c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by MitoTracker staining data shown in Figure 5c-d.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of TMRM staining was lower in NOTHC1-KD HAoSMCs than in the WT group under rhythmic strain, indicating loss of mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: As shown in Figure 5e–f, the fluorescence intensity of the tetramethylrhodamine methyl ester perchlorate (TMRM) staining, which reflects the mitochondrial membrane potential, was lower in NOTHC1-KD HAoSMCs than in the WT group under rhythmic strain. These results indicated loss of mitochondrial membrane potential in NOTCH1-KD HAoSMCs under rhythmic strain.
evidence: The claim is supported by TMRM staining data shown in Figure 5e-f.

claim: The mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX) staining of NOTHC1-KD HAoSMCs was significantly higher than that of the WT group under rhythmic strain, indicating that ROS production was increased.
source: The mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX) staining of NOTHC1-KD HAoSMCs was significantly higher than that of the WT group under rhythmic strain (Figure 5g–h), which indicated that ROS production was increased in NOTCH1-KD HAoSMCs under rhythmic strain conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by MitoSOX staining data shown in Figure 5g-h.

claim: Rhythmic strain increased the ATP concentration in both WT and NOTHC1-KD HAoSMCs, but under rhythmic strain conditions, a lower ATP concentration was found in NOTCH1-KD HAoSMCs than in WT HAoSMCs.
source: Rhythmic strain increased the ATP concentration in both WT and NOTHC1-KD HAoSMCs, but under rhythmic strain conditions, a lower ATP concentration was found in NOTCH1-KD HAoSMCs than in WT HAoSMCs (Figure 5i).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP concentration measurements shown in Figure 5i.

claim: No significant difference in the TMRM or MitoSOX fluorescence intensity or ATP concentration was found between WT and NOTCH1-KD HAoSMCs under static conditions.
source: No significant difference in the TMRM or MitoSOX fluorescence intensity or ATP concentration was found between WT and NOTCH1-KD HAoSMCs under static conditions, which indicated that NOTCH1 insufficiency did not affect mitochondrial function under static conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of TMRM, MitoSOX, and ATP.

claim: NOTCH1 insufficiency could induce mitochondrial dysfunction in HAoSMCs by reducing mitochondrial fusion, inducing loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, increasing ROS production and generating insufficient ATP under rhythmic strain.
source: Taken together, these data indicated that NOTCH1 insufficiency could induce mitochondrial dysfunction in HAoSMCs by reducing mitochondrial fusion, inducing loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, increasing ROS production and generating insufficient ATP under rhythmic strain, and these effects are accompanied by an impaired contractile phenotype.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Imbalanced mitochondrial dynamics could induce VSMC dedifferentiation into the synthetic phenotype.
source: These findings were consistent with previous studies showing that imbalanced mitochondrial dynamics could induce VSMC dedifferentiation into the synthetic phenotype (Salabei and Hill, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Salabei and Hill, 2013.

claim: All three drugs (Mdivi-1, leflunomide, teriflunomide) enhanced MFN1 and MFN2 expression to different extents in CRL1999 HAoSMCs.
source: In the model using CRL1999 HAoSMCs (Figure 6b), all three drugs enhanced MFN1 and MFN2 expression to different extents, and the greatest increase in MFN1 expression was obtained with Mdivi-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by drug screening data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The three drugs all decreased DRP1 expression to different extents but did not affect MFF expression in CRL1999 HAoSMCs.
source: In addition, the three drugs all decreased DRP1 expression to different extents but did not affect MFF expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by drug screening experimental data.

claim: The three drugs increased SM22 and CNN1 expression to different extents in CRL1999 HAoSMCs, and the maximal expression of SM22 and CNN1 was obtained with leflunomide.
source: The three drugs also increased SM22 and CNN1 expression to different extents, and the maximal expression of SM22 and CNN1 was obtained with leflunomide.
evidence: The claim is supported by drug screening experimental data.

claim: All three drugs enhanced MFN2 expression to different extents in BAV-TAA p-HAoSMCs, and maximal MFN2 expression was obtained with the treatment of teriflunomide.
source: The three drugs exerted different effects on mitochondrial dynamics-related proteins (Figure 6e–g). All three drugs enhanced MFN2 expression to different extents, and maximal MFN2 expression was obtained with the treatment of teriflunomide.
evidence: The claim is supported by drug screening data shown in Figure 6e-g.

claim: The three drugs increased MFN1 expression and decreased DRP1 expression to different extents in two lines of BAV-TAA p-HAoSMCs, and the greatest decrease in DRP1 expression was obtained with teriflunomide.
source: The three drugs increased MFN1 expression and decreased DRP1 expression to different extents in two lines of BAV-TAA p-HAoSMCs, and the greatest decrease in DRP1 expression was obtained with teriflunomide.
evidence: The claim is supported by drug screening experimental data.

claim: Teriflunomide significantly increased SM22 expression in the two lines of BAV-TAA p-HAoSMCs.
source: The three drugs decreased MFF expression to different extents in the two lines of BAV-TAA p-HAoSMCs and exerted different effects on the expression of the contractile proteins SM22 and CNN1, and teriflunomide significantly increased SM22 expression in the two lines of BAV-TAA p-HAoSMCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by drug screening experimental data.

claim: All three drugs enhanced CNN1 expression to different extents, and Mdivi-1 or teriflunomide significantly increased CNN1 expression in one line of BAV-TAA p-HAoSMCs.
source: All three drugs enhanced CNN1 expression to different extents, and Mdivi-1 or teriflunomide significantly increased CNN1 expression in one line of BAV-TAA p-HAoSMCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by drug screening experimental data.

claim: Teriflunomide exerted a more obvious effect on rescuing impaired mitochondrial dynamics and the expression of the contractile phenotype proteins SM22 and CNN1 under rhythmic high-strain conditions in BAV-TAA p-HAoSMCs.
source: Overall, the data from BAV-TAA p-HAoSMCs indicated that teriflunomide exerted a more obvious effect on rescuing impaired mitochondrial dynamics and the expression of the contractile phenotype proteins SM22 and CNN1 under rhythmic high-strain conditions.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from drug screening experimental data.

claim: Leflunomide, Mdivi-1, and, in particular, teriflunomide, could serve as drug candidates for ameliorating the disease progression of BAV-TAA.
source: These results indicated that leflunomide, Mdivi-1, and, in particular, teriflunomide, could serve as drug candidates for ameliorating the disease progression of BAV-TAA.
evidence: The claim is a speculative conclusion based on experimental drug screening data.

claim: The aorta smooth muscle-on-a-chip model could apply a biomimetic rhythmic tensile strain with a confined amplitude/magnitude and rhythm to HAoSMCs.
source: We showed that this model could apply a biomimetic rhythmic tensile strain with a confined amplitude/magnitude and rhythm to HAoSMCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental characterization of the on-chip model.

claim: Impaired mitochondrial fusion contributed to the attenuated contractile phenotype observed in NOTCH1-KD HAoSMCs.
source: We also confirmed that impaired mitochondrial fusion contributed to the attenuated contractile phenotype observed in NOTCH1-KD HAoSMCs.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from experimental observations on the on-chip model.

claim: MFN1/2 agonists and DRP1 inhibitors were able to reverse the imbalance in mitochondrial dynamics and partly rescue the contractile phenotype in NOTCH1-insufficient HAoSMCs.
source: We further identified that MFN1/2 agonists and DRP1 inhibitors were able to reverse the imbalance in mitochondrial dynamics and partly rescue the contractile phenotype in NOTCH1-insufficient HAoSMCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by drug screening experimental data.

claim: Patients with BAV-TAA presented lower expression of NOTCH1 protein in ascending aortic aneurysms.
source: Using clinical samples, our protein analysis also indicated that patients with BAV-TAA presented lower expression of NOTCH1 protein in ascending aortic aneurysms
evidence: The claim is supported by protein analysis of clinical samples.

claim: The NOTCH1 insufficiency was accompanied with attenuated mitochondrial fusion in BAV-TAA patients.
source: and the NOTCH1 insufficiency was accompanied with attenuated mitochondrial fusion.
evidence: The claim is supported by protein analysis of clinical samples.

claim: NOTCH1 regulates mitochondria dynamics in cardiovascular cell differentiation and survival.
source: This was consistent with the previous studies that reported NOTCH1 regulates mitochondria dynamics in cardiovascular cell differentiation and survival.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Mitochondrial fusion regulates the differentiation of myocardial cells through NOTCH1 signaling pathway.
source: Kasahara et al. found that mitochondrial fusion regulates the differentiation of myocardial cells through NOTCH1 signaling pathway (Kasahara et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kasahara et al., 2013.

claim: NOTCH1 insufficiency induced mitochondrial dysfunction in HAoSMCs by reducing mitochondrial fusion, along with loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, increasing ROS production and generating insufficient ATP under rhythmic strain.
source: Here, we found that NOTCH1 insufficiency induced mitochondrial dysfunction in HAoSMCs by reducing mitochondrial fusion, along with loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, increasing ROS production and generating insufficient ATP under rhythmic strain.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from experimental observations.

claim: Decreased contractile phenotype was found in NOTCH1-deficient HAoSMCs under rhythmic tensile strain and in BAV-TAA aortic tissues, accompanied by lower NOTCH1 expression and impaired mitochondrial fusion.
source: Consistently, we found decreased contractile phenotype in NOTCH1-deficient HAoSMCs under rhythmic tensile strain and in BAV-TAA aortic tissues, accompanied by lower NOTCH1 expression and impaired mitochondrial fusion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from both on-chip model and tissue analysis.

claim: NOTCH1 signaling is involved in the regulation of HAoSMCs differentiation and the expression of contractile proteins.
source: NOTCH1 signaling is also involved in the regulation of HAoSMCs differentiation and the expression of contractile proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge.

claim: HAoSMCs are highly plastic cells and undergo reversible changes in phenotype in response to environmental stimuli.
source: HAoSMCs are highly plastic cells and undergo reversible changes in phenotype in response to environmental stimuli (Vásquez-Trincado et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vásquez-Trincado et al., 2016.

claim: Most healthy HAoSMCs in the vascular wall in vivo exhibit a contractile phenotype, which allows them to maintain vascular tone.
source: Most healthy HAoSMCs in the vascular wall in vivo exhibit a contractile phenotype, which allows them to maintain vascular tone (Milewicz et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Milewicz et al., 2008.

claim: Decreases in α-SMA, MYH11, SM22, and CNN1 attenuate HAoSMCs contractility unit formation and further disrupt force generation, promoting the development of aortic aneurysm or dissections.
source: Decreases in α-SMA, MYH11, SM22, and CNN1 attenuate HAoSMCs contractility unit formation and further disrupt force generation, promoting the development of aortic aneurysm or dissections (Gillis et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gillis et al., 2013.

claim: HAoSMCs transform from a contractile into a synthetic phenotype and induce loss of vascular tone, which is one of the major pathological process in TAA.
source: HAoSMCs transform from a contractile into a synthetic phenotype and induce loose of vascular tone, which is one of the major pathological process in TAA.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about TAA pathology.

claim: The enhancement of HAoSMCs contractility is indicative of the effectiveness of pharmacotherapy for controlling aortic aneurysm.
source: Thus, the enhancement of HAoSMCs contractility is indicative of the effectiveness of pharmacotherapy for controlling aortic aneurysm (Oller et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oller et al., 2021.

claim: NOTCH1 insufficiency in HAoSMCs downregulated the contractile phenotype proteins SM22 and CNN1 under rhythmic strain.
source: In this study, we found that NOTCH1 insufficiency in HAoSMCs downregulated the contractile phenotype proteins SM22 and CNN1 under rhythmic strain.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The expressions of SM22 and CNN1 were decreased in BAV-TAA aortic tissues compared to non-diseased aortic tissues.
source: Also, the expressions of SM22 and CNN1 were decreased in BAV-TAA aortic tissues compared to non-diseased aortic tissues.
evidence: The claim is supported by protein analysis of tissue samples.

claim: NOTCH1 activation was needed for expression of the contractile phenotype protein αSMA in VSMCs via the NOTCH/CSL axis.
source: Noseda et al. reported that NOTCH1 activation was needed for expression of the contractile phenotype protein αSMA in VSMCs via the NOTCH/CSL axis (Noseda et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Noseda et al., 2006.

claim: NOTCH1 promotes the differentiation of the cardiac neural crest into differentiated VSMCs and the expression of αSMA.
source: High et al. reported that NOTCH1 promotes the differentiation of the cardiac neural crest into differentiated VSMCs and the expression of αSMA (High et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to High et al., 2007.

claim: NOTCH1-insufficiency reduced the contractile phenotype through decreasing mitochondrial fusion.
